name: autogen

facts.description: A programming framework for agentic AI

title: AutoGen: A Python Framework for Agentic AI
answer: AutoGen is Microsoft's open source Python framework for building multi-agent AI applications, released in 2023 and now at version 0.4. It sits above model APIs, orchestrating agents that converse, call tools, and run code. The one thing to know before adopting it: it is a fast-moving project with a migration guide between major versions, so pin your version and budget time for upgrades.

sections.body: AutoGen is a programming framework for agentic AI, made by Microsoft and distributed as the open source repository microsoft/autogen under a CC-BY-4.0 licence. It is written in Python and first appeared in 2023, with version 0.4 released later and accompanied by a migration guide. It sits in the orchestration layer of the AI stack, above raw model APIs and below the application. Rather than calling a model once, it lets you define agents that hold conversations, invoke tools, execute code, and hand work to one another, so it is the layer where multi-agent behaviour is designed and run. The official site states it is the official project and is not affiliated with any forks or startups.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The framework is used for concrete AI jobs that involve more than a single prompt. Its documentation shows enhanced inference through autogen.OpenAIWrapper for openai>=1 and autogen.Completion as a drop-in replacement for openai.Completion and openai.ChatCompletion on openai<1, with benefits including performance tuning, API unification, caching, error handling, multi-config inference, result filtering, and templating. It is used for local model work, demonstrated with FastChat serving ChatGLM2-6B through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and for research systems such as MathChat, a conversational framework using GPT-4 for advanced mathematics, and AutoDefense, a multi-agent jailbreak defence built on AutoGen. It is strongest where several agents with distinct roles must collaborate, and where code execution and tool use are part of the loop.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve is moderate. A developer needs working Python, a grasp of how LLM APIs are called, and enough familiarity with asynchronous and event-driven code to follow agent conversations. The documentation assumes you can configure model access, for example by passing an llm_config argument to an agent constructor with a config_list of dictionaries containing keys such as model, api_key, base_url, and tags. No deep mathematics is required for ordinary use apart from understanding inference hyperparameters like temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and n. The official site offers a migration guide, topic pages, and blog posts, but a beginner should expect to read several pages before a first agent runs.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The project is large and active, with roughly 61,000 stars on GitHub and a last push in April 2026. Its ecosystem includes integrations such as AgentOps, described on the site as the official agent observability tool, which is enabled by setting an AGENTOPS_API_KEY and calling agentops.init(), and which tracks LLM calls, costs, latency, agent failures, multi-agent interactions, and tool usage from one dashboard. The documentation covers LLM configuration, enhanced inference, and use cases, and the blog carries research and tutorial posts. Community material includes worked examples with FastChat, ChatGLM2-6B, and the openai-python library, though some of that content targets the older 0.2 line.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: AutoGen is built for both quick experiments and controlled production use, and the trade-off is complexity. A single agent with an llm_config can be running in minutes, which suits prototyping. For production, the config_list supports multiple models, and an agent uses the first available model, retrying against the second and so on if a request fails, which gives resilience against throttling. Filtering by tags and the use of deepcopy on llm_config to avoid internal mutation show attention to operational detail. The cost is that configuration, observability, and version migration become real work, and the site notes that agents generally contain no hidden logic to pick the best model for a task.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: AutoGen is a current standard rather than a legacy choice, backed by Microsoft and used in research systems such as MathChat and AutoDefense, and in enterprise settings through the AgentOps integration, which the site frames as making AutoGen trustworthy in production with monitoring and logging. Its star count and active repository indicate a broad developer base. For someone choosing what to learn, it is a reasonable bet for agent engineering roles, though the facts and the site do not give adoption figures by company or industry, so claims about specific employers would go beyond what is documented.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: AutoGen is a Python framework and is typically used alongside model providers and serving tools rather than replacing them. The documentation shows it working with OpenAI and Azure OpenAI endpoints, with custom endpoints identified by a model name such as llama-7B, and with local serving through FastChat, which exposes OpenAI-compatible APIs so a local model can act as a drop-in replacement for OpenAI APIs with minor code changes. It also works with the openai-python library and with autogen.code_utils and autogen.math_utils for evaluation. The polyglot pattern is therefore Python orchestration on top of whatever inference stack a team already runs, whether hosted or self-hosted.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The framework is fast moving, and the site itself points readers of the 0.2 documentation to a 0.4 migration guide, which means older tutorials and examples may not run unchanged. Some documented workarounds, such as commenting out finish_reason lines in FastChat protocol files, are fragile. The site does not state benchmark results for agent tasks, does not give a formal support policy, and does not say how the CC-BY-4.0 licence applies to production deployments, so those questions remain open. It also does not claim that agents automatically choose the best model, and notes that specialised agents may attempt it, which leaves model selection largely a design decision.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
